sections.title: Where did it begin?
sections.body: I first encountered aptamers in 2013. My initial assignment was cell-based aptamer selection. Nobody in the group had succeeded at it before, and everyone was reluctant to take it on. Students in my cohort under Professor Tan were required to start with selection. None of us wanted to; I felt the same, but did not dare say so. I gave myself three months: if it worked, I would continue; if not, at least I would have tried. To my surprise, it worked within three months. Aptamers have been part of my life ever since. Over time, I became increasingly aware of bottlenecks in the selection methods themselves and devoted much of my time to developing new methods. As high-throughput sequencing advanced, cell-SELEX began generating enormous datasets. I kept wondering: what could we uncover through aptamers' ability to be sequenced, an advantage antibodies do not have? Single-cell sequencing-based Apt-seq could capture binding patterns across multiple cell types in one experiment, using barcode-like profiles to describe cell surfaces across multiple parameters, almost like facial recognition for cells. That was exciting.

sections.title: What challenges did I encounter?
sections.body: There were so many challenges. With my background in biology, I did not know how to analyze the enormous sequencing datasets, let alone explore them in depth. The data were right in front of me, but I could not understand them. That felt deeply frustrating. I tried to teach myself, but progress was slow, and at one point I wondered whether I had chosen the wrong direction. Eventually, I realized I could not do it all alone. I needed to collaborate with people working in bioinformatics and learn from the beginning how to turn data into something we could explain clearly. It was one of the most awkward, but also most honest, periods of my research life.

sections.title: What did we ultimately discover?
sections.body: We eventually established the single-cell Apt-seq platform, and students in our group can now follow the workflow themselves. Its significance is this: where aptamer screening previously depended on repeated wet-lab experiments, a single sequencing experiment can now read binding patterns on the surfaces of multiple cell types, almost like building a facial-recognition profile for each cell. Aptamers' ability to be sequenced has finally become more than a source of abundant data. It is now a tool whose output we can understand and reuse, allowing others to pick up the work and take it further.

sections.title: What would I like to explore next?
sections.body: Apt-seq enables simultaneous detection of multiple molecules on the cell membrane. Many directions are worth exploring, including applying Apt-seq to a specific biological question and obtaining aptamers for more membrane proteins. Above all, I want to understand what these aptamer-sequencing-based barcodes can actually be used for.

sections.title: 从哪里开始？
sections.body: 2013年我开始接触核酸适体。最初的任务是做细胞核酸适体筛选，课题组此前没人成功过，大家都不敢碰。我们那届谭老师的学生被要求必须先做筛选，没人愿意，我也一样，只是不敢说。我给自己定了三个月：做出来就继续，做不出来也算试过了。没想到三个月真做出来了。从那时起，我就和核酸适体纠缠上了。后来我越来越意识到，筛选方法本身还有不少卡脖子的问题，于是把大量时间投入方法开发。高通量测序技术发展起来后，cell-SELEX产生了海量数据。我常想：核酸适体可测序这个抗体比不了的优势，到底能挖出什么？基于单细胞测序的Apt-seq能一次性获得多种细胞的结合模式，像条形码一样给细胞表面做多参数描绘，实现“人脸识别式”检测——这太酷了。

sections.title: 遇到了什么困难？
sections.body: 困难太多了。首先我是生物背景出身，面对巨大的测序数据，我不会分析，也不会深入挖掘。数据摆在面前，我却读不懂它，那种感觉特别无力。我试着自己啃，进展很慢，一度怀疑这个方向是不是选错了。后来我意识到，靠一个人硬扛不行，得去找做生物信息的人合作，从头学起怎么把数据变成能讲清楚的东西。那段时间是我科研上最笨拙、也最真实的一段。

sections.title: 最终发现了什么？
sections.body: 最终我们把单细胞Apt-seq平台搭起来了，现在课题组的学生都能照着做。它的意义在于：以前筛适体靠一次次湿实验去试，现在一次测序就能同时读出多种细胞表面的结合模式，像给细胞“刷脸”建档。适体可测序这个优势，终于从“数据多”变成了“能读懂、能复用”的工具，别人接手就能往下走。

sections.title: 接下来想探索什么？
sections.body: Apt-seq可以同时实现细胞膜上多个分子的同时检测，未来值得探索的方向很多，包括将Apt-seq应用于一个具体的生物学问题，以及获得更多膜蛋白的适体等等，最希望进一步探索的是基于核酸适体测序的这些条形码究竟有什么用？
